mappings.note: Electron dot structure of CO2, a simple carbon compound. LO-4 verbatim.

Electron dot structure of S8. The skill is LO-4's, but LO-4 is worded for CARBON compounds and sulphur is not one, so the competency C 1.3 (representing substances with symbols) is cited instead of stretching the outcome.
Counts the structural isomers of pentane. The isomer clause of LO-4.
The two properties of carbon behind the huge number of its compounds -- catenation and tetravalency. LO-3 restated.
Formula and electron dot structure of cyclopentane. Drawing a carbon compound, LO-4.
Draws ethanoic acid, bromopentane and butanone, then asks whether bromopentane has isomers. Structures and isomers, LO-4; the naming is given, not asked, so not LO-4 of C 1.1.
Names given compounds. Nomenclature within a homologous series, C 1.1-LO-4. The structures themselves are not rendered by the tool, but the demand -- naming -- is unambiguous.
Why ethanol to ethanoic acid counts as oxidation. LO-8 names both compounds; this is its central reaction.

Ethyne burned in oxygen rather than air, for a hot non-sooty flame. Combustion of hydrocarbons has no learning outcome in this frame, so the C 1.3 competency on chemical changes is cited rather than forcing LO-3 or LO-4.
Bench test separating an alcohol from a carboxylic acid (litmus, carbonate fizz). Properties of ethanol versus ethanoic acid, LO-8.
Definition of an oxidising agent, asked in the abstract. No LO in this frame covers redox terminology; cited at C 1.3, which owns describing chemical changes.
Whether a detergent can test for hard water -- it cannot, because detergents lather regardless. That soap/detergent contrast is LO-9.
Why clothes must be agitated -- to detach micelle-trapped dirt. Cleansing action, LO-9.
Number of covalent bonds in ethane. The count follows from carbon being tetravalent and hydrogen univalent, which is LO-3; nothing has to be drawn, so not C 1.3-LO-4.
Butanone's functional group is a ketone. Functional-group identification, LO-4.
A blackened vessel means incomplete combustion. Combustion has no outcome in this frame; cited at the C 1.3 competency.
Nature of the covalent bond shown through CH3Cl -- carbon sharing all four valence electrons. Tetravalency, LO-3; the question asks for the bonding idea, not a drawn structure.
Defines a homologous series with an example. LO-4 word for word.
Distinguishes ethanol from ethanoic acid on physical and chemical grounds. LO-8's core.
Why micelles form in water and not in ethanol. Micelle formation, LO-9.
Why carbon compounds serve as fuels -- clean, high-calorific combustion. No combustion outcome exists here, so the C 1.3 competency on chemical changes is cited.
Scum when soap meets hard water. The hard-water failure of soap, which LO-9 covers through the soap/detergent distinction.
Litmus test on soap, showing it is basic. A property of the soap itself, so LO-9 rather than LO-8, which is about ethanol and ethanoic acid.
Hydrogenation and its use in hardening oils. An addition reaction; the frame has no outcome for hydrocarbon reaction types, so the C 1.3 competency is cited.
Picks the hydrocarbons that add (C3H6, C2H2). The discriminator is saturated versus unsaturated, i.e. which homologous series each formula belongs to -- LO-4.
Test telling butter from cooking oil -- bromine water, i.e. saturated versus unsaturated. Series identification, LO-4.
Mechanism of soap's cleansing action. LO-9 verbatim.

Names A, B, C in the ethene -> ethane -> chloroethane chain (LO-4) and asks for the equation and reaction type, which is the C 1.3 competency since addition and substitution have no outcome of their own.
Names the functional group that can be hydrogenated (LO-4) and then describes the reaction with its conditions and product change, cited at C 1.3 for want of a hydrogenation outcome.
C2H6O used for sterilising skin, oxidised by alkaline KMnO4 to the two-carbon acid -- ethanol to ethanoic acid. LO-8.

Reads six structural formulae to group them by family and pick out the non-hydrocarbons. Family grouping is C 1.1-LO-4; reading the structural formulae is C 1.3-LO-4. The figures are not rendered by the tool, but both demands are stated in the stem.
(a) Bromine water decolourised by ethene but not methane -- unsaturation, LO-4. (b) Splits an ester back into its acid and alcohol, which is the esterification clause of LO-8.
The form in which carbon occurs in the atmosphere. Occurrence has no outcome in this frame -- LO-3 is tetravalency and catenation, not abundance -- so the C 1.1 competency is cited.

Carbon compounds are poor conductors with weak intermolecular forces. These properties follow from the covalent bonding that LO-3 addresses; C 1.2's competency text is about mixtures and separation, so it fits worse.
Bond types in ammonia. Not a carbon compound, so LO-4 of C 1.3 (which is carbon-specific) does not apply; cited at the competency.
Buckminsterfullerene is an allotrope of carbon. Allotropy is a direct consequence of carbon's catenation and tetravalency, LO-3.
Picks the correct chain isomers of butane from drawn structures. The isomer clause of LO-4.
Alkaline KMnO4 acting as an oxidising agent. The referenced reaction is not printed, but in this chapter alkaline KMnO4 appears only in the ethanol-to-ethanoic-acid oxidation, so LO-8.
Names the reaction type when oils are hydrogenated to fats (addition). Reaction typing has no LO here; cited at C 1.3.
Which of four compounds carries -OH (butanol). Functional-group identification, LO-4.
Soap has a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tail. The structural basis of micelle formation, LO-9.
Electron dot structure of nitrogen. Not a carbon compound, so the carbon-specific LO-4 does not fit; cited at the C 1.3 competency.
Structural formula of ethyne. LO-4.
Identifies propene and propyne as unsaturated from their names. Homologous-series membership, LO-4.
Chlorine substitutes into alkanes in sunlight. Reaction conditions for substitution, which has no outcome in this frame; cited at C 1.3.
Orientation of the ionic end and carbon chain in a micelle. LO-9 verbatim.
Number of covalent bonds in pentane. Same reading as the ethane item: it falls out of carbon's tetravalency, LO-3.
Structural formula of benzene. LO-4.
Ethanol with sodium gives sodium ethoxide and hydrogen. A named reaction of ethanol, LO-8.
Correct structural formula of butanoic acid. LO-4; the name is given, so no nomenclature is being tested.
Vinegar is 5-8 per cent ethanoic acid in water. A property of ethanoic acid, LO-8.
Why mineral acids beat carboxylic acids in strength -- complete versus partial ionisation. The weak-acid character of ethanoic acid, LO-8.
Carbon reaches the neon configuration after four shared bonds. Tetravalency, LO-3.
Electron dot structure of water. Not a carbon compound, so cited at the C 1.3 competency rather than the carbon-specific LO-4.
Picks the branched structure from drawn hydrocarbons. Reading structural formulae and chain branching, LO-4.
Which drawn hydrocarbons are unsaturated. The verdict is series membership (alkene/alkyne), so C 1.1-LO-4 rather than the drawing outcome.
IUPAC name of CH3-CH2-CHO. Naming from the functional group, LO-4.
Identifies oxygen and bromine as the heteroatoms. Heteroatoms are what define functional groups, LO-4.
Spots C3H6 as the odd one out of an alkane series. Homologous-series membership, LO-4.
First member of the alkene family (ethene). Homologous series, LO-4.
